strengths: Provides a self-contained derivation of a dynamical mean-field theory for kernel/random-feature regression with power-law eigenvalue spectra, using the MSRDJ formalism and a variational Gaussian approximation.
Unifies several training regimes in one framework: gradient flow with/without weight decay, Langevin dynamics, and the stationary Bayesian Gaussian process limit.

Derives explicit effective equations for mode-wise learning, the response/memory kernel, the effective correlated noise, and the test error, yielding interpretable order parameters and a mode-decoupling picture.

Simulations in Figures 1-4 show good agreement with the theoretical predictions for mode dynamics, test-error evolution, bias-variance decomposition, and early stopping under different temperatures and regularization strengths.
Gives an intuitive explanation of early stopping and regularization as a bias-variance trade-off, and identifies a disorder-induced memory kernel that slows learning.
The discussion acknowledges the linearized nature of the setup and outlines plausible future extensions to feature learning.
weaknesses: The central claimed contribution on 'neural scaling laws' and the bullet promising 'analytical results that relate the power-law exponent of the feature kernel, regularization, and early stopping time to obtain a minimal generalization gap' are not delivered. The manuscript does not derive a scaling-law exponent or a minimal-generalization-gap formula, and no experiments vary the power-law exponent or data/model size to exhibit scaling laws.

The claim that the variational Gaussian approximation becomes exact in the large-N limit is asserted rather than rigorously justified. The dropped higher-order terms and non-Gaussian corrections are treated heuristically, with no finite-size analysis, error bounds, or convergence guarantees.

Relative to prior work such as Bordelon et al. (2024, 2025), the technical advance appears incremental: it adds L2 regularization and Langevin noise and re-derives known dynamical mean-field equations for random-feature regression, while the more distinctive promised scaling-law results are absent.

Numerical validation is limited to N=P=100, a single power-law exponent eta_i ~ i^{-3/2}, and no exploration of the P/N ratio, finite-size effects, or large-system scaling. The asymptotic claims are therefore not stress-tested.

Presentation and internal consistency need improvement: equation numbering is confusing, the test-error definition (29) uses C(t,s) rather than C(t,t), and some notation/parameter descriptions (e.g., beta vs 2 beta^{-1}, Lambda_{ij} vs eta_i) are inconsistent across figures and text.

The paper lacks an explicit early-stopping-time formula or a quantitative comparison to prior theoretical predictions or real neural-network scaling laws, making the connection to actual neural scaling behavior speculative.

No code or detailed simulation reproducibility package is provided; while parameters are listed, the many self-consistent equations and disorder averages would be difficult to reproduce exactly without further implementation details.

strengths: The paper derives a self-consistent dynamical mean-field theory for the learning dynamics of kernel/feature regression using the MSRDJ formalism plus a variational Gaussian approximation (VGA), and organizes the physics into a small set of self-averaging order parameters (R, C, C̃). The resulting effective description (Eq. 19–28) is clean: eigenmodes decouple into independent stochastic processes coupled only through a memory kernel K and a shared effective noise, with a closed-form Fourier-domain solution for the Green's function (Eq. 24).

The framework is genuinely general along two axes: β interpolates between Langevin/SGD-like noise and deterministic gradient flow, and gβ interpolates the L2 regularization, while the t→∞ limit connects to the Bayesian/GP posterior. Even if the individual limits are known, packaging them into one dynamical derivation is useful.

The bias–variance decomposition of the test error (Eq. 30) and its use to explain early stopping under noise with power-law spectra is a clear, interpretable result, and the qualitative explanation of why weight decay mainly suppresses the variance term at late times (Sec. 4.3, Fig. 4) is reasonable.

Numerical experiments with 10^5 disorder realizations at P=N=100 corroborate the theory for mode-wise discrepancy (Fig. 1), test-error dynamics across β (Fig. 2), bias–variance components (Fig. 3), and regularization strength (Fig. 4). The agreement is qualitatively convincing for the regimes shown.

The identification of the resummed response K as an Onsager-like reaction term that slows learning, and the observation that slow modes indirectly slow down all other modes, is a nice physical interpretation of the spectral bias.
weaknesses: The headline claim is not delivered. The title and abstract promise 'neural scaling laws' and 'analytical results that relate the power-law exponent of the feature kernel, regularization, and early stopping time to obtain a minimal generalization gap,' but the paper never derives or even plots a scaling law (loss vs. P or N at fixed training) nor the claimed closed-form relation between exponent, regularization and optimal stopping time. The actual results are all test-error-versus-training-time curves; the central selling point is unsupported.

Novelty relative to prior work is thin and insufficiently differentiated. Bordelon, Atanasov & Pehlevan (2024, ICML) already derive a dynamical DMFT for random-feature regression with power-law spectra and obtain neural scaling laws; Canatar et al. (2021) cover the static power-law kernel case; Seung et al. (1992) and Naveh et al. (2020) already establish the Bayesian/GP-posterior interpretation of the Langevin stationary distribution. The incremental additions here (L2 regularization, a response-function analysis, and the noise-temperature axis) do not obviously clear the bar, and the 'unification' is largely a reparametrization via limits of β and g rather than a conceptual advance.

The claim that the VGA becomes exact in the large-N limit ('the central limit theorem guarantees the Gaussianity of the process') is asserted, not proven. The disorder-averaged action contains a non-Gaussian log-det term, and no argument or numerical evidence for vanishing approximation error with N is given; the mode-resolved variational ansatz with mode-dependent G_i makes exactness especially non-obvious.

The numerical evidence is limited and does not test the large-N claim. Simulations are at P=N=100 with a single power-law exponent (γ=1/2), and visible deviations between theory and simulation appear in the high-noise/late-time regime (e.g., the β=10 curve in Fig. 2), with no systematic finite-size study of how the theory-simulation gap scales with N.

Presentation issues reduce reliability: Eq. (29) writes L_test = (1/2)C̄(t,s) rather than C̄(t,t); order parameters and kernels are named inconsistently across main text and appendices (R̃ vs R̄, G_i^{(vṽ)} vs G_i); the appendix is disorganized; and figure quality is low (small, low-resolution panels), making the quantitative agreement hard to verify.

Reproducibility is under-specified: no code or data availability statement, and key simulation details (teacher weight distribution, feature sampling, integration scheme for the self-consistency) are only partially given, so the numerical claims are hard to reproduce independently.

Framing is somewhat loose: the model is Gaussian-design linear/kernel regression on a fixed feature map, but it is repeatedly called 'random feature regression' and linked to NNGP/NTK universality without addressing how the Gaussian-feature and fixed-kernel assumptions limit the relevance to the phenomena the abstract invokes.

strengths: Provides a genuinely useful unification: a single dynamical mean-field theory (MSRDJ field theory + variational Gaussian approximation) that recovers gradient flow with/without weight decay, Langevin stochastic training, and—at equilibrium—Bayesian inference on the induced Gaussian process. This is a clean and non-trivial synthesis of regimes that prior work (Advani et al., Krogh & Hertz, Maloney et al.) treated separately.

The effective description is compact and interpretable: the N modes decouple and interact only through a collective memory/response kernel K(t-s) (a resummed geometric series of the system's response, Eq. 21/56) and a shared, self-consistently determined colored noise (Eq. 20/59). Reducing the dynamics to essentially two self-averaging order parameters (the response R and autocorrelation C) is a meaningful simplification over approaches that require auxiliary fields (e.g., Bordelon et al., 2024).

The bias-variance decomposition of the test error (Eq. 30) yields a clear and convincing mechanistic account of early stopping: the bias term decays monotonically while the variance grows with time, producing an interior optimum, and stronger L2 regularization mainly suppresses the long-time variance (Figs. 3 and 4). This is a nice, physically interpretable result.

The theory is validated against direct simulations across several parameter regimes (Figs. 1-4), with simulation settings (dt, P, N, number of disorder realizations) reported, supporting the core claims at intermediate times.

The paper is honest about its scope, explicitly restricting to linearized/kernel settings and pointing to feature-learning work (Li & Sompolinsky; Seroussi et al.; Rubin et al.) as necessary next steps.
weaknesses: The claimed quantitative agreement is somewhat overstated. In Fig. 2 (notably the blue β=10 curve) and Fig. 1, theory (dashed) and simulation (solid) visibly diverge at late times, and the paper does not analyze or quantify the source of this discrepancy (finite P=N=100, finite dt, or a genuine breakdown of the theory). For a paper whose headline claim is to 'quantitatively explain the dynamics of the generalization error,' this warrants more careful treatment.

Several introduction-level claims are not clearly delivered in the main text—in particular the promise of 'analytical results that relate the power-law exponent of the feature kernel, regularization, and early stopping time to obtain a minimal generalization gap.' No such closed-form scaling relation appears to be derived or validated, so the framing around 'neural scaling laws' is looser than the abstract/bullet list suggests.

Novelty is incremental relative to Bordelon, Atanasov & Pehlevan (2024/2025), which the authors themselves identify as the closest work. The main differentiators—adding L2 regularization and Langevin noise, and obtaining a more compact set of order parameters—are useful but modest extensions rather than a fundamentally new understanding.

The assertion that the variational Gaussian approximation becomes exact in the large-N limit because 'the central limit theorem guarantees the Gaussianity of the process' is stated rather than justified; the exactness of the VGA is a substantive technical claim that deserves a more rigorous argument or at least careful hedging.

Notation is inconsistent across the main text and figures (e.g., η_i in Eq. 9 vs. Λ_ij = δ_ij η_i in the appendices and figure captions, with Λ_ij = i^{-3/2}δ_ij implying γ=1/2). Combined with dense, appendix-heavy exposition, this makes the paper harder to follow and to reproduce than necessary.

The practical and scientific reach is limited by the idealized linear/kernel setting; while acknowledged, the paper does not demonstrate that the derived dynamics capture any quantitative feature of real trained networks beyond the qualitative early-stopping effect.

strengths: Complete, self-contained derivation of a dynamical mean-field theory for Langevin/gradient-flow training of kernel (random-feature) regression with power-law spectra, via the MSRDJ formalism plus a variational Gaussian approximation; the VGA-exactness argument in the N→∞ limit is given (Appendix C), and the noiseless stationary limit is shown analytically to reproduce Canatar et al. (2021) (Appendix I), which is a strong consistency check.

The resulting theory is interpretable: decoupled per-mode equations of motion coupled only through a memory kernel K and a self-consistently determined correlated effective noise; the bias-variance decomposition of the test error follows naturally (Eq. 32) and is used to give a dynamical explanation of early stopping. Theory and simulation agree across several settings (Figs. 1–3, Fig. 6), with simulation details (dt, number of disorder realizations) reported.

Concrete, quotable new predictions: the optimal stopping time t* = (β/2)·α/(1+α), claimed independent of P and N, and L_test(t*) ~ d1 (Pβ)^{-α/(1+α)} − d2 N^{-α}. The β-dependence of t* is checked against simulation (Fig. 5) and the P-dependence of the minimal loss in the inset of Fig. 4.

Honest and appropriate treatment of limitations: the linearized/kernel restriction is stated, the importance of finite-size corrections for the optimal-loss estimate is explicitly acknowledged, an impact statement is included, and an extension path (label noise in Appendix H, committee machines in Appendix J) is sketched.

The framework does cover several training regimes in one SDE (β→∞ gradient flow with/without weight decay; t→∞ Gibbs/Bayesian posterior with label noise; finite-β Langevin), and the connection between Langevin noise and the Bayesian posterior (Appendix F) is made explicit.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to closely related work that the paper itself cites: Bordelon et al. (2024) already derive a dynamical model of neural scaling laws for random-feature regression with power-law spectra and compute-optimal Pareto frontiers (Volterra equations), and Canatar et al. (2021), Maloney et al. (2022), Paquette et al. (2024) cover much of the static/scaling ground. The 'unification' is largely the observation that gradient flow, weight decay and the Gibbs posterior are limits of a single Langevin SDE, which is standard; the claimed advantages ('fewer and more interpretable order parameters', 'no auxiliary fields') are asserted but never benchmarked (no comparison of accuracy/compactness against the cited DMFT).

The headline early-stopping result (36) is derived only in the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck limit K(t−s) ≈ δ(t−s) (Section 5.1, Appendix G), i.e. it discards precisely the disorder-induced memory kernel that the paper advertises as a central contribution ('explain how the analytically found, disorder induced, effective self-coupling slows down the learning dynamics'). No figure quantifies this slowdown (full theory vs. OU approximation is never compared), so a claimed contribution remains unsupported.

Because the memory kernel and effective noise are P-dependent, the claimed P-independence of t* is not obvious beyond the OU approximation, and it is not directly tested: Fig. 5 varies only β at fixed P = N = 100. Moreover, Fig. 4 (which varies P = 50…300) appears to place the minima at roughly comparable compute (Pt) rather than comparable time, which would contradict the claimed P-independence. A dedicated P-sweep of the measured t* is needed.

Verification is narrow. Every numerical experiment uses a single spectral exponent (η_i = i^{-3/2}, i.e. α = 1/2), so the theory's dependence on α — the core of both (36) and (37) — is never tested. System sizes are small (N = 100, 1000), and the paper concedes that 'finite size effects play an important role in correctly estimating the optimal generalization error', which weakens the quantitative scaling claims; the P-scaling is supported by only a few points over a narrow range (inset of Fig. 4) with no fitted exponents reported, and the finite-N floor N^{-α} is described as dominating over wide ranges.

Presentation and care are insufficient for a main-track submission: the related-work section leaves unresolved placeholder citations ([1], [2], [10], [11]), the reference list is garbled (e.g. 'Lee and Sonnolz (2018)', 'Martin and Siggia (2021)' for Martin, Siggia & Rose 1973, missing years/venues, a future-dated 'Coppola et al., 2026' absent from the list), the exponent is denoted γ in Eq. (9) but α throughout Section 5 and the appendices, Section 4.2 cross-references an appendix equation ('the mean given by (61)') instead of (27), and the discussion's claim of 'two self-averaging order parameters' conflicts with the three defined in (19) (R, C, C̃).

Generality/realism of the assumptions is asserted rather than demonstrated: the theory rests on the Gaussian-feature (Wishart) assumption plus the orthogonality relation (8), and the relevance to real networks with structured, correlated feature kernels and feature learning is motivated only by citation (e.g. 'Coppola et al., 2026'). Reproducibility is only moderate: the self-consistent numerical solution of the theory is described loosely (dt = 10^{-2}) and no code is provided.

strengths: Provides a unified dynamical mean-field theory for kernel regression with power-law spectra, covering Langevin dynamics, gradient flow, and Bayesian inference.
Derives effective equations of motion for modes, response functions, and test error, showing decoupling of modes and self-averaging.
Derives scaling laws for bias and variance, and an explicit formula for optimal early stopping time t* = β/2 * α/(1+α).
Numerical simulations show good agreement with theory for the chosen parameters.
Recovers known stationary results from Canatar et al. (2021) in the appropriate limit.
Extends to label noise and outlines extension to committee machines.
Honest limitations discussion.
weaknesses: Missing citations: References [1], [2], [3], [4], [10] are cited in the text but not defined in the reference list, making the related work section incomprehensible.
Notation inconsistency: Power-law exponent denoted as γ in eq (9) but as α in Section 5 and appendices, with no definition of α in main text.
Figure captions refer to legends that are not present (e.g., Fig 1), and figures are small and hard to read.

The early stopping formula t* is derived under the OUP approximation and high-noise limit; its independence from P and N is not validated by simulations (only β is varied in Fig 5). The paper claims independence from P,N but provides no evidence.
Scaling laws are tested only for one exponent α=1/2 (η_i = i^{-3/2}). No validation for other exponents.
The theory is for linear regression with Gaussian features; the connection to neural scaling laws is speculative and not directly validated on neural networks or real data.
No code or detailed algorithm for solving the self-consistent equations is provided, hindering reproducibility.
Minor mathematical error: In Appendix G.2, they state c3 = (1+α)c1, but a factor of 2 is missing (c3 = 2(1+α)c1). This doesn't affect the scaling exponents but indicates carelessness.
The paper claims 'fewer and more interpretable order parameters' than Bordelon et al. 2024, but no direct comparison is provided.
The paper does not compare numerically to Bordelon et al. 2024, which is the closest related work.

strengths: Derives a comprehensive dynamical mean-field theory for Langevin training in kernel regression with power-law kernel eigenvalues, unifying Bayesian inference, gradient flow with/without weight decay, and stochastic Langevin dynamics in a single framework.

Provides a compact and interpretable effective description: the N eigenmodes decouple and interact only through a collective memory kernel and an effective correlated noise; the test error is naturally expressed as a single order parameter C(t,t).

Obtains an analytical bias-variance decomposition of the test error and explains early stopping; derives a simple optimal stopping time t* = (β/2) α/(1+α) and an optimal generalization error scaling law.
Recovers known stationary results (Canatar et al.) and extends them to dynamics; connects the analysis to neural scaling laws and the compute-optimal Pareto frontier.

Numerical simulations support the theoretical predictions across different noise levels, regularization strengths, and sample sizes; the appendices provide detailed derivations of the MSRDJ action, VGA, and scaling laws.
Discusses extensions to label noise and committee machines, and includes an impact statement and a limitations discussion.
weaknesses: Notation inconsistencies: the power-law exponent is denoted γ in Eq. (9) but α in the scaling-law section; the relation c3 = (1+α)c1 in Eq. (35) appears off by a factor of 2; and the solid/dashed line conventions for theory vs. simulation are inconsistent between figures.

The claim that for P,t→∞ the bias recovers L ∼ N^{-α} is problematic: in the N-dimensional teacher-student setup, the bias vanishes as P,t→∞, so the N^{-α} term is an artifact of the asymptotic expansion valid only for Pt ≪ N^{1+α}, not a true irreducible loss. This should be clarified or corrected.
The independence of the optimal stopping time t* from P and N is not empirically verified; Fig. 5 varies only β while fixing P=N=100, so finite-size dependence cannot be ruled out.

The theory assumes Gaussian features, orthogonality, and no feature learning; while acknowledged in the Discussion, the abstract and introduction may overstate applicability to neural networks and neural scaling laws given the linearized setting.
Reproducibility could be improved by releasing code or providing more details about the simulations, although the main parameters, step sizes, and number of disorder realizations are given.
The main text is dense and relies heavily on appendices; some key derivations, such as the exactness of the variational Gaussian approximation in the N→∞ limit, are only sketched in the main text.
